prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, based on magic-wavelength trapping of atoms, which brought the measurement of time and frequency into a new regime of precision.

statement.case_for: I keep B010 with Katori and Ye, and the first-round exchange has sharpened rather than weakened my reasons. The core is one physical idea. At the magic wavelength the lattice light shifts the two clock levels equally, so the atoms can be held tightly enough to remove Doppler and recoil shifts while thousands of them are read out together. That removes the old trade-off between atom number and systematic shifts. Katori proposed it and made the first demonstrations. Ye's group carried it to the 1e-18 regime and into spin-exchange and many-body physics inside the clock. What I value most is that the numbers do not rest on one laboratory. Strontium clocks at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL are compared with each other, and the shifts that limit them are understood in atomic-structure terms: polarizabilities, magic wavelengths, blackbody and higher-order light shifts. The results already do physics. They resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres and bound drifting constants. I do not count the pending redefinition of the second as part of my case. It is a metrology decision, and Eriksson and Pearce are right that it should not set the timing. A prize built from these two people is also the cleanest attribution on the shortlist. I stress that I did not choose it because five members now agree. Three of those five moved after the opening ballots, and agreement reached that way is not evidence. I choose it because the case survives the questions I would ask of any result.
statement.case_against: The objection I cannot dismiss is the one Kroll, Pearce, Johansson and Mehlig all raise. The 2005 prize gave the frequency comb, the 2012 prize gave control of single ions and the Al+ clock, and a sceptic can read the lattice clock as the next step in a line already honoured. I also accept, as Eriksson and Pearce do, that this is a measurement capability rather than a surprise about nature. Third, Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg, the Kimble-era magic-wavelength discussion and the ion-clock groups lie outside the credited names, and a two-person prize cannot fix that. My answer to the first point is that neither earlier prize contains the lattice scheme, so the citation must name magic-wavelength trapping explicitly. If the committee regards the earlier prizes as having largely covered optical clocks, my case becomes weaker and I would want to hear that argument made against the specific lattice contribution. I would then rank IceCube above clocks, because a first observation in nature is a different kind of achievement.

responses.point: Eriksson asks whether the blackbody-shift uncertainty is now settled well enough that the 1e-18 claim is independently secure, and says the redefinition of the second should not drive timing.
responses.response: I agree on timing and have taken the redefinition out of my argument. On blackbody radiation I can give a qualified answer from the atomic-structure side. The shift scales with the static polarizability difference and a small dynamic correction, and for strontium these have been evaluated by calculation and measured separately, and they agree within stated uncertainties. More importantly, the two groups no longer rely on the coefficient alone. JILA characterises the thermal environment of the atoms in situ, and the Tokyo group has operated a cryogenic lattice clock in which the radiation field is cut by orders of magnitude. Clocks with different strategies agree at the 1e-18 level, and that agreement does more for me than any single coefficient. I would still say that the best 1e-18 claims are not equally robust, and I recall this from memory and not from the expert reports. The citation should therefore name the magic-wavelength lattice and the accuracy regime, and avoid naming a single record figure.

responses.point: Pearce asks how much weight I give the 2005 and 2012 prizes and argues that the citation must name the magic-wavelength lattice, not time and frequency in general.
responses.response: I accept your wording point fully, and my revised citation now says magic-wavelength trapping. On weight, I give the earlier prizes real weight but not decisive weight. The comb was a tool for counting optical cycles and the 2012 citation concerned manipulating single quantum systems. Both made optical clocks possible, and neither contained the idea that lets many atoms be trapped without shifting the transition. That is a distinct invention with a distinct set of systematics, and the many-body regime Ye's group reached has no counterpart in the single-ion work. I would not claim the lattice clock is as large as either earlier prize. I claim only that it is a separate achievement with its own credit. If the expert reports show that the lattice scheme was effectively already in hand before Katori's work, I would reconsider.

responses.point: Mehlig revises his earlier low ranking of B010, finds the attribution cleaner than any topological configuration, but keeps a conceptual hesitation because the enabling tools already received the 2005 and 2012 prizes. He still prefers B047.
responses.response: I value your honesty about the conceptual point, and I share part of it. Where I disagree is that I would not call B010 a fallback for the case where the topological allocation fails. Your own case is also strong, because Kane and Mele supply a mechanism that can be stated precisely and Molenkamp's experiment closed the loop. My difficulty with B047 is not the physics but the credit and the date. With Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and Hasan outside the names, and the 2016 prize covering the conceptual core, I fear the award would look like a partial reward for a field the committee has already recognised. I do not think a cleaner credit alone should decide a prize, but when both candidates are scientifically mature I give it real weight.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube as a discovery in nature and notes that B010 has broader support and cleaner attribution, and asks implicitly what the lattice clock has revealed that earlier clocks could not.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge, and I will answer it as an atomic physicist. Earlier clocks could not show gravitational redshift across a millimetre-sized sample, and could not make the interactions among interrogated atoms a controlled and measured part of the clock. Both follow from interrogating thousands of atoms at once with extreme coherence, and both are results about nature, not just better numbers. They are still modest next to opening a new window on the universe, and I do not pretend otherwise. I keep IceCube as my main alternative. What holds me back is the attribution you acknowledge: Halzen, Karle and Spiering come from a collaboration of hundreds, and I cannot tell from my own field which of them was decisive for the 2013 observation. If the expert reports answer that clearly, I would move B061 up, and I would encourage you to say what evidence you think would settle it.

responses.point: Olsson asks, for the lattice clock, who made the original contribution between Katori and Ye and whether the redefinition of the second should be awaited.
responses.response: I would say Katori made the conceptual contribution, the magic-wavelength lattice, together with the first demonstrations in strontium. Ye's group made the contribution that turned it into the most accurate clocks and showed what many interrogated atoms can do. These are different kinds of credit and I do not think either can be ranked above the other, so I would give the two names equal standing in the citation. Awaiting the redefinition would, in my view, confuse a scientific question with a standards decision. The science is mature now. I also take your point that your own candidate, aberration-corrected microscopy, is a real achievement and not weak. My concern there is the omitted STEM-corrector line, which you raise yourself, and an instrument prize where the credit has to be drawn through two parallel developments.

uncertainties: Whether a majority of the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. If not, I would move toward IceCube.
Whether the expert reports confirm the priority I recall for Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstrations, and how they weigh Lemonde, Takamoto and the Kimble-era discussion.

My statements about blackbody-shift evaluations in strontium come from memory of the atomic-structure literature, not from the expert reports, and the most extreme 1e-18 claims may be less independent than the best-characterised ones.
Whether the evidence on IceCube source identification and on who was decisive in 2013 is strong enough to change my ranking, since this lies outside my own field.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier, a 2023 laureate, and work in attosecond physics, but that concerns B054, which is not on this shortlist. My own field of atomic many-body theory is close to the structure calculations behind lattice clocks, and I have no personal or institutional link to Katori, Ye, RIKEN, JILA or any other credited person on the shortlist that I can identify. I know the ultracold-atom community behind B019 only from a distance. I see no need for recusal on any shortlisted part.
